name: USA
sub: Typical single-stream curbside Recycling, Trash and (where offered) Compost, plus hazardous-waste drop-off, pharmacy take-back and store drop-off for plastic bags.

banana.w: Food scraps go in a compost cart where your city has one; otherwise they go in the trash.

eggshell.w: Egg shells compost well; use the trash if your city has no compost collection.

coffee.w: Coffee grounds and paper filters go in compost where it is offered, otherwise in the trash.

bones.w: City compost programs usually take bones, but home compost piles don't; without a program, use the trash.

shampoo.w: Empty plastic bottles are accepted in almost every curbside recycling program.

polybag.w: Plastic bags jam sorting machines, so keep them out of the recycling cart. Many grocery stores collect them.

chips.w: Chip bags are made of layered plastic and foil, which most programs cannot recycle.

tube.w: Most US programs don't accept toothpaste tubes yet, even the ones labelled recyclable.

carton.w: Most US households can recycle milk cartons at the curb, but some programs still don't take them.

eggtray.w: Paper egg cartons are usually recycled with paper, or composted where a compost program takes them.

box.w: Flatten cardboard boxes and put them in the recycling cart.

pizza.w: Scrape out the food and recycle the box. Put heavily soiled parts in compost or the trash.

newspaper.w: Newspapers are one of the easiest things to recycle.

jar.w: Glass jars are recycled in most programs, but some cities want glass taken to a separate drop-off.

wine.w: Wine bottles go in recycling; a few cities require glass drop-off, and some states refund a deposit.

perfume.w: Most programs take only food and drink glass, and the spray pump can't be removed.

tin.w: Rinse food cans and put them in the recycling cart.

window.w: Broken glass can injure sorting workers, and window glass melts differently. Wrap it and put it in the trash.

drinkglass.w: Drinking glass differs from bottle glass, and broken pieces are a hazard. Wrap them and put them in the trash.

mirror.w: Mirrors have a coating and can't be recycled; wrap broken pieces and put them in the trash.

tissue.w: Used tissues go in the trash; some city compost programs accept them.

diaper.w: Disposable diapers go in the trash; they are not recyclable or compostable at the curb.

pad.w: Wrap sanitary pads and put them in the trash; don't flush them.

battery.w: Most places allow alkaline AAs in the trash, but EPA recommends recycling them at a drop-off. Never put them in recycling.

bulb.w: CFLs contain mercury, so take them to a hazardous waste drop-off or a hardware store take-back.

meds.w: Use a pharmacy drop box. With no take-back nearby, FDA says seal pills in a bag with coffee grounds and trash them.

paint.w: Take oil-based and leftover paint to a drop-off; in many places dried-out latex paint can go in the trash.

toy.w: Broken plastic toys aren't accepted in curbside recycling, so they go in the trash.
